name: Attendance and Early Warning
title: Attendance and Early Warning
answer: Attendance and early warning means using data to spot rising absences or risk of failing or dropping out, then having a person follow up. It matters because chronic absence is one of the clearest warning signs that a student is struggling, and messaging alone is only part of the answer. The flag starts a conversation, it does not label the student.

sections.body: This idea pairs attendance data and early warning predictions with a human response. A student information system can flag students whose absences are rising, and an attendance worker, counselor, or teacher follows up. Early warning systems predict which students are at risk of failing or dropping out. The problem it solves is that messaging about absences helps but is not enough on its own, and data alone cannot know why a student is missing school. The person who follows up may learn that a student is caring for a sick parent, being bullied, or missing the bus.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school, a student information system can flag students whose absences are rising. An attendance worker, counselor, or teacher then follows up, and the follow up might be a call home, a meeting, or a visit. Early warning systems predict which students are at risk of failing or dropping out. Machine learning can improve these predictions, but it takes expertise to use well. The text does not give separate grade band examples, so the practice is described for schools generally.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text does not attach a formal evidence label, but it reports that chronic absence is one of the clearest warning signs that a student is struggling. Messages to parents about their child's absences reduce chronic absence, with effects of 10 to 15 percent in the original trials and smaller effects in newer ones run at scale (Rogers & Feller, 2018; Robinson et al., 2018; Berger et al., 2025). A meta analysis of 13 recent studies of attendance interventions found a small average effect, stronger when carried out within a single school (Li, 2026). Machine learning can improve early warning predictions, but it takes expertise to use well, and results from systems whose reasoning is hidden can be read through staff members' existing biases (Soland et al., 2020). Interviews with students whose risk predictions were wrong found that the errors came from sudden life events, such as family changes, health problems, or computer trouble (Hlosta et al., 2022).
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: Early warning flags should never follow a student as labels. A flag is a reason for a conversation, not a judgment about who a student is. Staff should be trained to see flags this way. Students and families should never be told that a computer has decided a child is at risk. Predictions are also wrong in ways that matter, and hidden reasoning can be read through staff members' existing biases, so the follow up and the decision stay with a person.
